prompt:
A 64-year-old man with established coronary artery disease (prior myocardial infarction) has an LDL cholesterol of 128 mg/dL. He reports genuine myalgias that resolved off statin and recurred on two separate statins at low doses, without CK elevation or rhabdomyolysis. What is the appropriate approach to lipid-lowering therapy?

Provide a stepwise therapeutic management plan including medications, counseling, and follow-up.

rubric_items.text: Offer a shared-decision trial of a different low-dose or intermittent statin regimen if acceptable to the patient, without delaying indicated nonstatin therapy.
Add ezetimibe if statin tolerance remains limited.
Add a PCSK9 inhibitor if LDL remains above goal on maximally tolerated therapy.
Set an LDL goal appropriate for very-high-risk secondary prevention, such as below 55–70 mg/dL.
Reinforce the need for ongoing lipid-lowering therapy because of his very high cardiovascular risk.
Consider bempedoic acid as an additional nonstatin option.
Evaluate for secondary or contributing causes of myalgia, including hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, and drug interactions.
Reinforce comprehensive lifestyle measures for cardiovascular risk reduction.
Recheck a lipid panel after therapy changes to confirm response.
Continue a statin only at a dose the patient tolerates, or prescribe nonstatin-only LDL-lowering therapy if no statin regimen is tolerable.
Refer to a lipid specialist if an acceptable LDL level cannot be achieved because of medication intolerance.
Instruct the patient to report recurrent or worsening muscle symptoms during rechallenge.
Discontinue all lipid-lowering therapy because of statin intolerance.
Recommend only red yeast rice or over-the-counter supplements in place of guideline-directed therapy.
Continue a full-dose statin despite intolerable, reproducible myalgias without adjustment.
Dismiss the muscle symptoms because the CK level is normal.
Use niacin as the primary substitute for evidence-based LDL-lowering therapy.
Use fibrate monotherapy as the primary treatment for this elevated LDL level.
Rely on lifestyle modification alone despite established coronary artery disease.
Accept an LDL level of 128 mg/dL as adequate because of the muscle symptoms.
Defer pharmacologic LDL lowering unless the LDL level reaches 190 mg/dL.
Perform routine serial CK testing in the absence of new or worsening muscle symptoms.
Initiate LDL apheresis for an LDL level of 128 mg/dL without first using appropriate medications.
Add gemfibrozil to a statin regimen despite the increased risk of muscle toxicity.
